title: Electronic Circuit Parameters & Units
description: The six circuit parameters, their SI units, and how to convert between multiples and submultiples.
content_html:
What Are Circuit Parameters?

Every electrical circuit can be described using a set of measurable quantities called circuit parameters. In the OCR Cambridge National specification for Programmable Systems, six parameters are central: potential difference, current, resistance, capacitance, power, and frequency. Understanding what each one means — and being precise about its unit — is essential for every calculation and every exam question that follows. Understanding these parameters and their correct SI units is the foundation for every circuit calculation, because mixing up units such as milliamps and amps, or kilohms and ohms, is one of the most common causes of wrong answers in the exam.

The Six Parameters and Their Units

Potential difference (often called voltage) is the electrical "push" that drives current around a circuit. It is the energy transferred per unit of charge, measured in volts (V). Current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor; its SI unit is the ampere (A), commonly shortened to amp. Resistance opposes current flow and is measured in ohms (Ω). Capacitance is the ability of a component to store electric charge; it is measured in farads (F). Power is the rate at which energy is transferred or converted in a circuit, measured in watts (W). Finally, frequency describes how many complete cycles of an alternating signal occur per second, measured in hertz (Hz).

Key Fact

The six circuit parameters and their units are: potential difference — volt (V); current — amp (A); resistance — ohm (Ω); capacitance — farad (F); power — watt (W); frequency — hertz (Hz). These are the only units the OCR specification requires you to know for Topic Area 1.1.

Unit Multiples and Submultiples

Real circuits rarely use base units alone. A radio signal might have a frequency of 100 000 000 Hz — far easier to write as 100 MHz (megahertz). A capacitor might store 0.000 001 F, which is written as 1 µF (microfarad). The OCR specification requires you to work with six prefixes: mega (M) = 10⁶ (one million), kilo (k) = 10³ (one thousand), milli (m) = 10⁻³ (one thousandth), micro (µ) = 10⁻⁶ (one millionth), nano (n) = 10⁻⁹ (one billionth), and pico (p) = 10⁻¹² (one trillionth). These prefixes apply to any unit — so kilohms (kΩ), milliamps (mA), and nanofarads (nF) are all fair game in the exam.

Converting Between Multiples and Submultiples

To convert from a prefixed unit to the base unit, multiply by the prefix value. For example, 4.7 kΩ = 4.7 × 1000 = 4700 Ω; 330 µF = 330 × 0.000 001 = 0.000 330 F. To go the other way — from base unit to a prefix — divide. For example, 0.025 A = 25 × 10⁻³ A = 25 mA. A reliable method is to count the steps on a prefix ladder: moving from milli to kilo is six orders of magnitude, so divide by 10⁶. Practise converting in both directions because OCR exam questions will give values in mixed prefixes and expect consistent working.

Key Fact

The six prefixes in order from largest to smallest are: mega (M, ×10⁶), kilo (k, ×10³), milli (m, ×10⁻³), micro (µ, ×10⁻⁶), nano (n, ×10⁻⁹), pico (p, ×10⁻¹²). To convert to the base unit, multiply by the prefix value; to convert from the base unit, divide.

The OCR specification uses the term "potential difference" rather than just "voltage" because it is technically more precise. Potential difference refers to the difference in electrical potential energy per unit charge between two specific points — it is always measured between two points, never at a single point. "Voltage" is the everyday shorthand, and both terms appear in exam questions. In circuit calculations they are treated identically; the key thing is to use the unit volt (V) and the symbol V in all working.

One of the most common errors in exam papers is mixing up lower-case m (milli, 10⁻³) with upper-case M (mega, 10⁶). They differ by a factor of one billion. Writing 1 mW (milliwatt, one thousandth of a watt) when you mean 1 MW (megawatt, one million watts) would be a catastrophic error in an engineering context — and will lose marks in the exam. Always check the case of the prefix symbol in your answer.
exam_tip_html: In OCR R047 exams, unit questions often carry easy marks that students throw away by writing the wrong symbol. Always write the symbol exactly: Ω not ohms, Hz not hz, µ not u for micro. If a question gives a value in kΩ and expects an answer in Ω, show the conversion step explicitly in your working — examiners award method marks even if your final answer is wrong. For prefix questions, learn the ladder (M, k, — , m, µ, n, p) so you can count steps without memorising every power of ten.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The six circuit parameters are potential difference (V), current (A), resistance (Ω), capacitance (F), power (W), and frequency (Hz) — learn the unit symbol for each as an inseparable pair.
  • Six prefixes scale units up or down: mega (M), kilo (k), milli (m), micro (µ), nano (n), pico (p) — to convert to the base unit multiply by the prefix value; to go back, divide.
  • Case matters: lower-case m is milli (10⁻³) and upper-case M is mega (10⁶) — confusing them in an exam answer will cost marks.

glossary_terms.definition: The measurable electrical quantities that describe the behaviour of a circuit, each with a defined SI or SI-derived unit.
The energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit; measured in volts (V).
The opposition a component or material offers to the flow of electric current; measured in ohms (Ω).
The ability of a component to store electric charge, measured in farads (F).

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the correct SI unit for electrical resistance?
A) Volt (V)
B) Amp (A)
C) Ohm (Ω)
D) Watt (W)
State two circuit parameters that can be measured in a simple LED circuit.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: potential difference (voltage) / current / resistance / power. Accept correct unit symbol as evidence of the correct parameter. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A resistor is labelled 4.7 kΩ. Show clearly how to convert this value to ohms.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: identifies kilo (k) = 10³ or ×1000. 1 mark: correct multiplication: 4.7 × 1000. 1 mark: correct answer = 4700 Ω (unit required). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'frequency' as a circuit parameter and give one example of where frequency is an important consideration in an electronic system.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (2 marks): frequency is the number of complete cycles of an alternating signal per second (1 mark); measured in hertz (Hz) (1 mark).
Example (2 marks): for example, a radio receiver must be tuned to a specific frequency (e.g. 98 MHz) to pick up a particular station — if the circuit's filter is set to the wrong frequency, the signal will not be processed correctly (2 marks for specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example such as 'frequency is used in radios'). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is designing a timing circuit. The specification sheet for the capacitor they want to use states its capacitance as 470 nF.

Discuss the importance of understanding unit multiples and submultiples when selecting and using electronic components in a circuit design.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): a balanced discussion that covers at least two relevant factors with development. For example: without understanding that 470 nF = 470 × 10⁻⁹ F = 0.000 000 470 F, the student cannot substitute the correct value into a timing formula and will produce an incorrect design — this leads to the circuit operating at the wrong frequency (first factor, developed). Contrasted with: understanding prefixes also allows the student to compare components efficiently — a capacitor listed as 0.47 µF is the same as 470 nF, so recognising this prevents ordering the wrong component and wasting time and money (second factor, developed, with example applied to the scenario).
Secure (3–4 marks): two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to unit conversion or circuit design.
Developing (2 marks): one factor identified but not clearly explained or applied.
Emerging (1 mark): a single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
An engineering student claims that all electronic unit prefixes can be ignored in calculations as long as the correct formula is used.

Evaluate the extent to which this claim is valid, using examples of different circuit parameters and their common submultiples.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): a balanced evaluation that acknowledges the student's claim has a kernel of truth (the formula structure is independent of units) but is fundamentally wrong in practice. Arguments against: substituting 4.7 kΩ as 4.7 into V = I × R gives an answer 1000 times too small — if current is in amps and resistance must be in ohms, every prefix must be converted first or the formula produces a meaningless number (developed, with example). Also: component datasheets always use prefixes — a capacitor listed as 100 µF has a capacitance of 0.0001 F; failing to convert means circuit timing calculations, filter frequencies, and power dissipation calculations are all wrong. Arguments for (partial credit perspective): if a student works entirely within a consistent prefix system (e.g. all milliamps and kilohms) and scales the answer accordingly, the relative relationships hold — so there is a sense in which the formula structure is independent of the absolute prefix chosen. However, this requires deliberate consistency and awareness of the prefix used, not ignorance of it. A clear, substantiated judgement should be reached: the claim is not valid; understanding prefixes and converting to base units before substitution is essential for accurate circuit calculations.
Secure (5–6 marks): arguments on both sides with application and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): relevant points, largely one-sided, limited judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): basic points with little development. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is the correct unit for capacitance?
Which of the following prefix symbols represents 'micro' (10⁻⁶)?
A capacitor has a value of 100 µF. Converted to farads, this is _____ F.
The unit of frequency is the _____, with symbol Hz.
Match each circuit parameter to its SI unit.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of potential difference and its symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The SI unit of potential difference is the volt, with the symbol V.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric current and its symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The SI unit of electric current is the ampere (amp), with the symbol A.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of resistance and its symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The SI unit of resistance is the ohm, with the symbol Ω.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of capacitance and its symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The SI unit of capacitance is the farad, with the symbol F.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of power and its symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The SI unit of power is the watt, with the symbol W.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the SI unit of frequency and its symbol?
flashcard_questions.a: The SI unit of frequency is the hertz, with the symbol Hz.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the prefix kilo (k) mean, and what is its multiplier value?
flashcard_questions.a: Kilo means one thousand; its multiplier value is 10³ (1000).

flashcard_questions.q: What does the prefix micro (µ) mean, and what is its multiplier value?
flashcard_questions.a: Micro means one millionth; its multiplier value is 10⁻⁶ (0.000001).
4.7 kΩ equals 4700 Ω, because kilo means ×1000 so 4.7 × 1000 = 4700.

flashcard_questions.q: What prefix symbol represents mega, and what is its value?
flashcard_questions.a: The prefix symbol for mega is M (upper-case), and its value is 10⁶ (one million).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between milli (m) and mega (M) as unit prefixes?
flashcard_questions.a: Milli (m) is 10⁻³ (one thousandth), while mega (M) is 10⁶ (one million) — they differ by 10⁹.

flashcard_questions.q: What does potential difference measure in an electrical circuit?
flashcard_questions.a: Potential difference measures the energy transferred per unit charge between two points in a circuit.
